title: The caliphate ends, 1924
hook: the Ottoman caliphate is abolished by the new Turkish Republic

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muhammad Iqbal, the poet of khudi, the self that rises. Your line was: the self can rise. Did you put your line of hope where you could see it? Today, something very old comes to a stop. Day one thousand twenty-three.

The new parliament of the Turkish Republic has voted, and an office no longer exists. That night in Istanbul, the man who held it is told he must leave the country. He paints and plays music, and his title, as tradition tells it, reaches back to the first generation after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Before dawn he and his family are taken to a train heading west, into Europe. He will not come back. Far away, in India, in Egypt, in Indonesia, Muslims read the news in their papers. Some weep. Some shrug. Some start organizing to bring it back. Today: the caliphate ends.
screen: `THE PARLIAMENT HAS VOTED.` → `A PAINTER WITH AN ANCIENT TITLE.` → `A TRAIN WEST, BEFORE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Caliph comes from the Arabic khalifa, a successor or deputy. After the Prophet's death, Sunni Muslims hold, the community chose Abu Bakr as successor; Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet had named Ali. The title passed down, through dynasties and quarrels, until it rested with the Ottoman sultans. The same root reaches back into the Qur'an itself. In Pickthall's words, when God tells the angels about Adam: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." A khalifa. Over the centuries, how much real power the caliph held changed a great deal. Sometimes he ruled an empire. Sometimes the title was mostly a symbol. After the Ottoman Empire fell apart following the First World War, the new parliament in Ankara first ended the sultanate, kept a caliph without a throne for a short while, and then, once the Republic was declared, abolished the office entirely. The last caliph, Abdulmecid, went into exile. How did Muslims take it? Not in one way. In India, a movement had already campaigned hard to protect the caliphate, and it lost its cause overnight. Some scholars gathered to talk about naming a new caliph, and nothing came of it. Others said that a Muslim's faith had never depended on one office in Istanbul. Today Muslims still differ: some hope to see a caliphate again, others organize their religious life through mosques, scholars and councils, and they argue about it openly. The Qur'an says of power, in Pickthall's words: "Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt." An institution ends. Prayer goes on.
screen: `KHALIFA: A SUCCESSOR, A DEPUTY.` · `FROM EMPIRE TO SYMBOL.` · `THE REPUBLIC ABOLISHES THE OFFICE.` · `MUSLIMS ANSWER IN MANY WAYS.` · then, large: `THOU WITHDRAWEST SOVEREIGNTY FROM WHOM THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about institutions ending. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one institution you once counted on that has changed or disappeared. A school that closed. A shop that held your street together. A newspaper, a club, a congregation that merged, a tradition your family stopped keeping. Notice what it held for people, and who picked up that work when it was gone, or whether no one did. If you pray, you can hold Qur'an 3:26 in mind, that sovereignty is given and withdrawn. If not, just breathe and let the place come back to you. The bell holds the time.
The caliphate ends. The new Turkish Republic abolished the office of caliph, and the last caliph went into exile. Today's word.
Your line: an institution ends. Today, thank someone who keeps a small institution going, a club, a mosque, a library desk, while it's still there. Day one thousand twenty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims today organize religious life through mosques, scholars, councils and national religious bodies, and they hold differing views about whether and how a caliphate should exist.

original.note: Arabic: a successor or deputy; the title of the caliph, and the word in Qur'an 2:30.

trapdoor: what you thought: a caliph is a kind of king.
what it means: khalifa, a successor, the title that passed down from the first leaders after the Prophet until the Turkish Republic abolished it.
what a scholar hears: the same word God uses of Adam, a viceroy in the earth, and an office whose real power rose and fell for centuries.

notes: Editor pass: hook now opens on the vote rather than another place-name scene; the title's reach back to the first generation framed as 'as tradition tells it'; myth item 'Muslims everywhere responded the same way' replaced (repeated the pattern of 1019 and 1021); 'changed enormously' toned down.
Claims rule: the year 1924 appears only in the title; 'the First World War' is named as a period. Confirm.
Abdulmecid II as painter and musician, and his departure by train before dawn with his family: confirm.
'A title that reaches back to the first generation after the Prophet': Ottoman claim to the caliphate's continuity is itself debated; confirm the hook's wording.
The caliphate congresses (e.g. Cairo) described as 'some scholars gathered to talk about naming a new caliph, and nothing came of it'; confirm.
Present-day views given without ranking; changed 'many' to 'others' under the claims rule.
Khalifa as successor/deputy and its link to 2:30: standard; confirm.
Pickthall 2:30 and 3:26 quoted from memory, matching wording used elsewhere in this path; confirm.

Audit (2026-10-01): two serious fixes. (1) The sultanate was abolished by the Grand National Assembly in Ankara in 1922, before the Republic was proclaimed in 1923; the teach and a myth item credited the Republic, now corrected. (2) 'His community chose a successor' stated the Sunni account as fact; now names Sunni (Abu Bakr chosen) and Shia (Ali designated) views without ranking. Abdulmecid II's pre-dawn departure by car and train via Çatalca checked. Practice is close to day 1020's endings practice (both from the outline); Keeper may want them further apart.
